a.summary: The mutator has no reach into the wire bytes at all — every body handed to readBody is GZIPOutputStream output modulo three fixed one-byte edits — so the target cannot generate the one malformed shape that readBody silently accepts: a valid gzip member followed by non-member bytes.
a.failure_scenario: A hostile or buggy provider/CDN returns `Content-Encoding: gzip` with a valid member carrying `{"result":[...` followed by any trailing bytes (padding, a truncated second member, a re-transmitted fragment). readBody returns only the first member's bytes and throws nothing, so the caller parses a silently truncated JSON-RPC document. Neither the 14 seeds nor 11,162,719 fuzz executions can reach that byte sequence, because no mode emits a valid member followed by non-member bytes, and no test in the commit pins the behaviour.

b.summary: The harness's "encoding-header shape" selector models a multi-encoding response only as two separate field lines, so it cannot reach the RFC-canonical comma-joined form `Content-Encoding: identity, gzip`, which `isGzipEncoded` silently fails to recognise and hands the caller still-compressed bytes.
b.failure_scenario: A caching proxy or CDN in front of an RPC provider combines the two `Content-Encoding` field lines it received (or an origin writes `Content-Encoding: identity, gzip` / `gzip, identity` directly, both RFC-legal). `isGzipEncoded` returns false, `readBytes`/`readInputStream` return the raw deflate bytes unchanged, and the JSON parser is handed binary — an opaque parse failure on every response from that path, with no diagnostic pointing at the encoding. Neither the 14 seeds nor the 11,162,719 fuzz executions can produce that header, because no encoding shape in the harness ever puts two tokens in one field value.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.

claims_new_evidence.instructions: Does `b` cite evidence that `a` does not?

criteria.true: `b` names a file, test, command, observation, or reproduction that `a` does not mention.
criteria.false: `b` cites nothing beyond what `a` already cites, or cites nothing at all.
